grh_084cb841970fc38cfb79.title: Retreat To Kindness
paragraphs: Former Rivers End troublemaker Jim Bradley returns as a successful, hard-edged reporter determined to write a sensational feature on psychiatrist Dr. Bob Patterson. Bradley plans to expose the violence and mental illness in Patterson's childhood home, including his father's commitment to an institution and young Patterson's own brief jailing after striking his father while defending his mother. Christian, Judy and Patterson argue that publishing every painful fact would serve gossip more than truth and would needlessly hurt Patterson's elderly mother, but Bradley prides himself on having no sentimentality and insists that hurting people is sometimes part of being a good reporter. Bradley has also returned to collect the diary his own mother left for him, sealed away after her death. Reading it changes him: his mother wrote of her love for Jim and of her gratitude to Patterson for helping her understand that Jim needed to leave Rivers End and make his own life, even though she longed to call him home. Confronted with the private compassion he had dismissed in others, Bradley abandons the article and tells Christian he is leaving with something more important, having made his own 'retreat to kindness.'

This [[show|dr-christian|Dr. Christian]] broadcast aired on November 28, 1945. It is listed as episode 366 in the archive. [[org|org.8480b75bc0c36e4b|CBS Radio Network]] carried the broadcast. The cast includes Jean Hersholt and Rosemary De Camp. Other credited names include Bob Anderson as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 24 minutes. The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.b199d95f77b6c241|Vaseline]].

grh_08ee5661570e7b13191b.title: The New Sun
paragraphs: A dramatization of Japanese artist Taro Yashima's The New Sun recounts his opposition to militarism and fascism inside prewar Japan. His drawings criticize military domination, leading to arrest, interrogation and brutal treatment alongside other political prisoners, while his pregnant wife and comrades also suffer under repression. Persuaded to sign a false confession so he can leave prison and continue the struggle through his art, Yashima eventually reaches the United States and uses his freedom to describe the Japanese anti-fascist resistance and expose the system he escaped.
